Uniform Title: *Aśeṣakulavallarī* Author: Gaṇanāthabhaṭṭa Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No.: 5-4656 Reel No.: A 175/11
Description: The *Aśeṣakulavallarī* is by Gaṇananāthabhaṭṭa, a Brahmin of the Garga gotra, who states at the outset that his teacher was Mahādevabhaṭṭa.
The title *Bhaṭṭa* was conferred upon ministers by the kings of Kashmir and remained as a hereditary title for their male family members and descendants. It is possible—

Therefore, he was a Kashmiri. The style and nature of the work indicate that it was composed well after the eleventh century. He states that he is composing a liturgical manual (*paddhati*) based on the *Vāmakeśvaramata*, the root tantra of...

The Goddess Tripurāsundarī. Chapter One treats the visualization and worship of the Guru and the lineage. Chapter Two concerns the preliminary purificatory ablution (*snāna*). Chapter Three begins with the worship of the door to the place of worship. The text breaks off shortly thereafter. Notes: Revision 0: November 13, 2014. Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.
Country of Publication:
India 1a) Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious and venerable Mother Tripurāmbikā.
I bow to that Maheśvarī, in whose praise even the five-faced Lord, though he is the master of sovereignty, was himself rendered powerless.
Victorious is that most venerable Guru, the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance,
by whose instruction there arose in the lineage of Garga one whose lotus-feet were honored by the king of poets, who possessed easily accessible scriptures,
and whose footstool was graced by the crest-jewels of sovereigns of the earth.

Born of Samaja and Naya with great effort, that treasury of knowledge, Śrī Mahādevabhaṭṭa— who dwells in Virajā for the sake of worshipping Bhavānī, who is an ocean of all virtues, a kinsman to kings, and a benefactor of the world— resides there free from passion.

His son was Gaṇanāthabhaṭṭa, a servant at the feet of all virtuous poets, free from envy, a knower of the secrets of all Tantras, whose mind was fixed upon the lotus-feet of Aṣṭāsvara, and who was devoted to the worship of the Goddess.
Having observed this, I shall properly compose a manual (*paddhati*) for the entire creeper of the Kula, in accordance with the intention of the Goddess Śrīvāmikā.
Then, at the time of the rising of the elder brother of Garuḍa, having risen and sat down,
[he meditated] upon the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus on his own head.
Resembling a moonstone, with a face like the autumnal moon,
his chest was adorned with white garlands.
She shines with two arms adorned with the gestures of granting boons and protection.
His body is embraced from the right by his own Śakti, Gadā, who rests on her left lap and holds a red lotus in her right hand.

Having meditated upon one's own Guru, whose mind is delighted by the nectar of the lotus of wisdom, [one should say]: "I worship the Śrīpādukā of the couple, [Name] Ānandanātha and [Name] Śaktī Ambā. Thus, having worshipped mentally with scents, unbroken rice grains, and flowers, and having offered salutations and praise, one should obtain permission for the performance of the daily rites (*nityakarman*).
Having dismissed the venerable Guru to his own place, he tarries for the sake of his necessary duties.
Thus ends the first section, the Gurudhyānapaddhati, in the Aśeṣavallarī composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Gaṇanātha.
Then, having performed the cleansing of the teeth, the rinsing of the mouth, and so forth, one should carry out the rite of bathing (*snānakarma*).

That [bathing] is of many varieties, such as the *vāruṇa*, *bhasma*, and *astra* [bathings]. Having invoked the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb by means of the *kramitya* *kuśa*-mudrā, [one should perform the bathing] with the seed-mantra of the *Śrīmūlavidyā*.

Having remembered [the mantras] whose essence is the Śiva-tattva, having immersed oneself three times with the yoni-mudrā, and having performed an ablution over one's own head seven times, one should go to the bank of the Avamī, put on two unsoiled garments, apply the tripuṇḍra marks with pure ash, and perform the ācamana (sipping of water). The details regarding ācamana are stated elsewhere; it is not defective here.
One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with pure water that is free from taste and smell, devoid of insects,
foam, and bubbles, and which has been inspected;
one should touch the three [joints] with three [fingers] and the two roots [of the nose] with two [fingers].
In the heart, the throat, and the palate, the twice-born [classes] correspond to their respective numbers.
By drinking water even once, Śūdras and women attain purification.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the mantra of the sacred ash (bhasma).
The practitioner of mantras, having consecrated [the water] with the mantras prescribed for sprinkling,
should stir it with his left hand from the crown of the head down to the feet.
1b) During the sprinkled ablutions, the *tripuṇḍra* marks, consecrated with mantras,
should be applied three times using the divine ring held in the right hand.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] three times with the left hand while reciting the mantras,
one should draw [the vital breath] in through the remaining luminous [nostril] and retain it within as a kumbhaka.
Having washed away its internal impurities, one should fashion it with skill;
then, with the Kṛṣṇātamamantra, one should cast it upon a diamond stone.
Thus concludes the procedure for bathing.
It is declared that this brings about the destruction of all sins. For those who are unable [to perform the full ritual], there is the measurement of the five limbs. It is as follows:
one should wash the hands below the wrist, the feet up to the ankles, and likewise the face;
this is its measurement, and one should maintain it otherwise.
The ash-bath has thus been described; now the mantra-bath is being explained.
Having sprinkled the mantra-purified water with mantras as prescribed for the five-limbed sprinkling,
the ritual for the twilight worship (sandhyā-vidhi) is now described.

There, having performed the placement of the hand-limbs (*karāṅga-vinyāsa*), one should perform an ablution (*mārjana*) seven times on one's own head with water held in the left hand over which the root mantra has been recited seven times. Taking the remaining water, which is of the nature of Śiva, in the right hand, one should [visualize] the form of Kṛṣṇa through the washing away of the impurities from the *kṛkṣa-kumbha* and *niśilā* by means of the *piṅgalā*.

Having purged oneself, one should cast [the water] upon the diamond-stone (vajraśilā) situated to the south with the mantra *Hraḥ Astrāya Phaṭ*. Then, having drunk the water held in the right hand over which the root-mantra has been recited seven times, and having sipped water (*ācamana*), [one should recite]: *Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ Mārtaṇḍabhairavāya Prakāśaśaktisaṃhitāya Sa...*

"Obeisance with *svāhā* to the Sun, together with his retinue of planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, lunar days, and yogas. Having thus offered the *argha* to the Sun and entered, one should visualize a triangle, a circle, and a square there; then, having gratified Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka on the left and right of the circle respectively, [one should worship] in the intermediate directions starting from Īśāna within the triangle, circle, and square.

Having gratified the lineage of gurus as will be described up to the northwest (vāyavya) direction, and having gratified the seat of the seasons (*ṛtvāsana*) in the center of the triangle with the mantras to be mentioned, one should invoke the Blessed Ones according to the description to be given. Having meditated upon them accordingly, one should gratify them three times with the root mantra using a stream of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*). Then, in the corners [are] Kāmeśvarī and the others.

Having satisfied the three deities with the *samaya-vidyā*, one should satisfy them in the corners of the square while meditating upon the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*). The meditation is described in the venerable *Prapañcasāra*: "The goddesses, possessing necklaces of crystal and collyrium, tawny and radiant as fire, have their hands raised in the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons."
The limbs are said to be weak when the primary bodies [of the letters] are deficient.
Regarding the rule for their placement, it is stated in the Śrīsāmabhujangavalī: "The letter *ve* is in the heart; *ha* is in the northeast; *si* is at the head; and *ra* is in the night."

Having recited the mantra for the Vāyovarmapura (the wind-armor city) four times in the four directions, one should offer libations to the Bhagavatī. Then, having dismissed the Bhagavatī, one should begin the recitation of the Gāyatrī:
*Aiṃ tripurā devī vidmahe klīṃ kāmeśvarī dhīmahi sauḥ tanno vāme pracodayāt*.

Having thus repeated the Gāyatrī ten times and performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with "Haṃsaḥ So'ham," one should release the sacred water (*tīrtha*) and proceed to the place of sacrifice with speech restrained. Regarding the place of sacrifice, no specific restriction has been stated elsewhere: it may be on a mountain, at a shrine for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), near a *liṅga*, a tree, a battlefield, the waters of a lake, a confluence of rivers, a crossroads, or a formidable location—even in the presence of Śiva.
Having abandoned what has been spoken [by others], worship in one's own home is indeed prescribed for the seeker of liberation. And in the *Kālikā-mata*:
"For those with few desires, worship in the forest is beneficial for the sake of attaining success.
For those who are free from desire and seeking liberation, constant worship in the home is recommended.
The sacrifice should be performed even in the house of sages, chief ascetics, initiated ones, and the twice-born, using juices produced from grapes.
Thus ends the second chapter, the manual on the rules for bathing, twilight rites, libations, worship, and bathing, within the *Aśeṣakulavallarī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Gaṇanātha.
Now, the worship of the Sun (*sūryapūjā*). Having smeared an auspicious sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the courtyard with water,
the best of practitioners, seated there upon a seat facing the east,
should duly pay homage to his former guru and to Gaṇapati.

For the *tilaka* mantra originating from the *Prayoga*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandas*), Savitṛ is the deity, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the fourfold goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Hrāṃ on the two hands; Hrīṃ on the palms of the hands; Saḥ on the backs of the hands; Hrīṃ from the toes of the feet up to [the heart]; Hrīṃ from the secret place up to the throat; Saḥ from the throat up to the head—one should thus assign [the mantras]. Hrāṃ to the heart, namaḥ; Hrīṃ to the head, svāhā.
HŪM, Vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock; HRAIṂ, HŪM to the armor; HRĀṂ, Vauṣaṭ to the eyes; HŪM, Phaṭ to the weapon. Thus is the procedure for the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Thus, having deposited the body [within the heart], one should meditate upon the Hot-rayed One (the Sun).

I worship the Sun, who sits upon a red lotus, the sole ocean of all virtues, the sovereign of all worlds; who holds a pair of lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; who wears a crown of rubies, whose body has the luster of coral sprouts, and who possesses three eyes. Having thus meditated before one, [one should draw] the solar disc with saffron, vermilion, and other pigments.
Having smeared a circular shape, the son of Maṇḍala should fashion a triangle, a circle, and a square in the center for the *arghya*;
having worshipped the *hṛdaya* and other limbs in the previously mentioned locations therein, and having established the *arghya-āsana*, he should worship it with:
"Obeisance to the Fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten *kalās*. Then, [he should place] a copper vessel there.

Having installed [the vessel] with "Obeisance to the solar disc, the self of twelve digits," and having worshipped thus; having sprinkled it with pure water; having honored it with "Obeisance to the lunar disc, the self of sixteen digits";
and having worshipped the heart and other limbs, one should consecrate it seven times with the root mantra while employing the *trāsaka* mudrā.
One should sprinkle oneself and the sacrificial materials with that water. Then, one should worship the golden pedestal (*svarṇapīṭha*).
It is as follows: *laṃ* salutation to Prabhutā; *vaṃ* salutation to Vimalā; *raṃ* salutation to Rasā;
*haṃ* salutation to Paramamukhā—thus from the southeast to the center. [Salutation] to Dharma, the self of Skanda.

*Namaḥ*. Salutation to the Self of the filaments, which is Knowledge. Salutation to the Self of the pericarp, which is Dispassion. Salutation to the Self of the central circle (*kaṇikā*), which is Sovereignty. Thus, from top to bottom. *Rāṃ*, salutation to Dīptā. *Rīṃ*, salutation to Śūṣmā. *Rūṃ*, salutation to Jayā. *Raṃ*, salutation to Bhadrā. *Raiṃ*, salutation to Vibhūti.
*Namaḥ*. *Rāṃ*, salutation to Vimalā; *Roṃ*, salutation to Amoghā; *Raṃ*, salutation to Vidyutā;
*Raḥ*, salutation to Sarvatomukhī. Having thus worshipped the nine Śaktis in the centers of the petals starting from the east, [one should worship] with the entire mantra:
"Salutation to the seat of yoga consisting of valor and the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Thus, having worshipped with the entire mantra.
"aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Mārtaṇḍabhairava in his embodied form.
(2b) Thus, with his hands joined in a *añjali* gesture holding flowers, he should cause [the deity] to become present within this external maṇḍala through the flow of the channel (*nāḍī*).

Having invoked [the deity] and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having displayed the lotus-mudrā, and having worshipped with whatever offerings are available, one should place the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) in the corners starting from the southeast of the body of the deity according to the sequence of dissolution (*layāṅga*), and in the directions starting from the east of the eight-petaled lotus according to the sequence of expansion (*pathāṅga*):
*soṃ somāya namaḥ*; *vuṃ budhāya namaḥ*; *vṛṃ bṛhaspataye namaḥ*.
Śuṃ, salutation to Śukra; Aṃ, salutation to Aṅgāraka; Śaṃ, salutation to Śanaiścara;
Rāṃ, salutation to Rāhu; Keṃ, salutation to Ketu; Aṃ, salutation to Aruṇa. Hṛṃ. O Agni, [here are] the Dhenumudrā, Goṣiṣāṇamudrā, Trāsinīmudrā, and Manonmanīmudrā for the heart and the other limbs.

Having displayed [the offerings] in the manner previously described, one should meditate. Then, having filled [the vessel] with water along with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, incense, lamps, and food offerings, and having worshipped it with the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Taking the *argha* water, one should contemplate the identity of the wick of the *kāśa* grass with the nature of the Sun. E&

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ phīṃ saḥ*, to Mārtaṇḍabhairava, together with the Power of Radiance (*prakāśa-śakti*), accompanied by his retinue of planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, lunar days, and yogas; seated upon the throne of Śiva-Sūrya, whose essence is the power of Śiva (*śiva-śakty-ātmake*), O Śrī Mahākāmacaitanyeśvarī, [accept] this *argha* offering—*svadhā*. Having thus offered the *argha*, [perform] the lotus-gesture (*padma-mudrā*) and the mirror-gesture (*vimba-mudrā*).
Having displayed [the deity], recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, and offered the fruit of the recitation with argha water using the mantra to be mentioned later,
one should praise and prostrate. Then, having offered argha facing east and joined the image with the weapon-mantra (astra),
one should dissolve the radiant Lord into the Tārā at one's own heart by means of the saṃhāra-mudrā.

Having dissolved the limbs and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) [of the mantras], and having offered [the oblation] to Caṇḍa with the words "and so forth," he should wash his hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Thus ends the third section, the ritual manual for the worship of the Sun, in the *Aśeṣakulavallarī* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Gaṇanātha.

Now, the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*). Just as for the *vālā* [deity], one sprinkles [water] upon it; on its left, right, top, and bottom: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ* (Salutation to Gaṇapati). *Iṃ Kṣāṃ Kṣetrapālāya Namaḥ* (Salutation to Kṣetrapāla). *Oṃ Dvāraśriyai* (Salutation to the Goddess of the Door).

*Salutation.* Oṃ, salutation to the threshold (*dehalī*). Having worshipped thus, [he should place] his right foot [inside]. Having entered the light, [and having worshipped] nakedly in the corners: Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ Duṃ, salutation to Durgā; Oṃ Vaṃ, salutation to Vaṭuka;
Oṃ Kṣāṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Having worshipped thus, [he enters] the jeweled pavilion (*ratnamaṇḍapa*).

Having come to the western door, [at the face of the dissolution]... * * * obeisance to Kāmadeva. Oṃ vāṃ... obeisance to Pīṭhyā. Oṃ... obeisance. Then, at the doors, facing the jeweled pavilion, are Sarasvatī and the others, marked by the signs of the noose and the goad.
As it has been said in the Somabhujavallī: "Sarasvatī,
Śrī, Māyā, Durgā, and thereafter Kālī, then Svāhā and Śubhaṅkarī."
Having dispelled all obstacles with the Lokanetra mantra and having taken up consecrated grains (*siddhākṣata*) and flowers with the Nārāca mudrā, [one recites]:

*Oṃ apasarpantu ye bhūtā ye bhūtā bhuvi saṃsthitāḥ | vighnakartāro ye bhūtāste naśyanti śivājñayā ||* "Oṃ! May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth; those beings who are creators of obstacles shall perish by the command of Śiva."
Having cast [the mantra] ending with *hraḥ astrāya phaṭ* inside, and having provided a path for the obstacles that do not depart by contracting the left limb,
one enters within with the left foot leading, saying: *Oṃ brahmaṇe vāstvadhipataye namaḥ* in the center.
Then one should worship Indra and the other deities. As it is stated in the venerable *Prapañcasāra*:

"Indra, Agni, Yama, Niśācara (Nairṛta), Varuṇa, Anila (Vāyu), Śivādhipati (Īśāna), and Vidhi (Brahmā)—these should be worshipped in sequence, along with their respective castes, presiding deities, weapons, vehicles, and retinues. Their colors are yellow, tawny, smoky, white, smoky, white, and white."

In the absence of the red *kāśa* flower, the *keśara*, *vāsava*, and others are prescribed [as substitutes]. Furthermore, the mounts and so forth are as follows: *Lāṃ*—Salutation to Indra, the lord of the gods, whose mount is Airāvata, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand, who is endowed with power, together with his limbs and retinue. *Rāṃ*—To the one in the southeast, the lord of fire, mounted upon a ram, holding a spear in his hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs...

Homage to [him] together with his retinue. Śāṃ! Homage to Yama, lord of the pretas, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff in his hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs and his retinue. Kṣauṃ! Homage to Nirṛti, lord of the rākṣasas, mounted upon a horse, holding a sword in his hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs and his retinue. Vāṃ!

Salutation to Varuṇa, the lord of waters, mounted upon a crocodile, holding a noose in his hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs and retinue. Vāṃ! Salutation to Vāyu, the lord of vital breaths, mounted upon a deer, holding a goad in his hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs and retinue. Kuṃ! Salutation to Kubera, the lord of Yakṣas, mounted upon a human, holding a mace in his hand.

Salutation to the one endowed with power, together with his limbs and retinue. Hrīṃ! Salutation to Īśāna, the Lord of Knowledge, mounted upon a bull, holding a trident in hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs and retinue. Āṃ! Salutation to Ananta, the Lord of Nagas, holding a discus in hand, endowed with power, together with his limbs and retinue. Oṃ! To Brahmā.
"Salutation to the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipati), who is mounted upon a swan, holds a lotus in his hand, is endowed with power (Śakti), together with his limbs (Aṅgas) and his retinue.
Upon that [lotus], one should prepare a soft, reddish seat. Regarding the rules for the seat, it is stated in another Āgama:
"For the six [deities]—the Ram, the Tiger, the Bull, the Bear, the Horse, and the Earth—there are various seats for each of their respective ritual acts. The ground [is the seat] for the Earth.

Likewise, the horn of a rhinoceros, as well as the *ūrṇa* (wool) and that born of *vīra* grass, the cane, and the auspicious deer-skin—all these are recognized by the wise as seats that bestow both liberation and worldly enjoyment. Among these, one should prepare the most pleasing seat. Even though it is prohibited [to sit directly] on the ground, sitting there brings fear of kings and causes the destruction of one's lineage.

A seat made of bamboo causes disease; likewise, a wooden seat brings about suffering, and a stone seat bestows great misery. A seat joined with clay, flowers, or sprouts, as well as one made of grass, creates enmity. [The same applies to] seats made of sheep-skin, goat-skin, and so forth.
"She is the bestower of all accomplishments, such as liberation. Therein, having worshipped with "Obeisance to the Lotus-Seated One," one should worship the Śakti.

Now, [he is one] whose forehead-leaf is adorned with a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) fashioned from the eight fragrant substances (gandhāṣṭaka). Regarding the eight fragrant substances: in the *Prapañcasāra* it is said that they are of many kinds. Now, according to the Śākta tradition: sandalwood, camphor, agallochum, saffron, musk, yellow pigment (rocanā), cora, and [the eighth];
this is the "eight fragrances" (gandhāṣṭaka), which brings about the presence [of the deity] and causes delight to the world. Now, let us return to the subject at hand.

Seated upon a seat, his chest resplendent with the *prastanya* rhythm, his face adorned with marks of *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and flowers, and his mouth [resembling] a sword, a spear, and a bow, he should place the *namaḥ* mudrā for the gurus on his left and right sides.
Salutation to Gaṇapati. Salutation to Durgā. Salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Salutation to the supreme teachers, the gurus.

Salutation to the previously perfected gurus. Salutation to the primordial perfected gurus. Having thus bowed to these upon one's own head, one should perform the purification of the hands. [Question: Among the various ritual placements (*nyāsa*), why is the purification of the hands performed at the very beginning?
Having raised this doubt, it is stated in another scripture: "In that regard, O lady of excellent complexion, purification of the two hands must first be performed;
by means of them, one should purify all other objects in every ritual action. And so it is said in the *Mūlasūtra*:
"O Goddess, one should perform the purification of the hands with the *sarvāghavidyā*. It is as follows:"
Aṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers. Aṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers. Sauṃḥ, salutation to the two little fingers.

Aṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Āṃ, salutation to the two index fingers. Sauṃḥ, salutation to the hollowed palms. With three [repetitions], salutation to the palms. With those [three], salutation to the two sides of the forehead. Thus, again, perform the triple clap with the hand.

One should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*). Then, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Thereafter, one should perform the retention (*kumbhaka*) with sixty-four measures (*mātrā*), and exhale gradually with twice that [number]. Having thus performed the breath control, one should place the sixfold seat (*āsana-ṣaṭka*).
It is as follows:

*Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Tripureśvari Amṛtāya Vāmanāya Namaḥ*—thus at the feet. *Aiṃ Klīṃ Hsīḥ Tripurasundari Tāmbujāya Namaḥ*—thus at the knees. *Hrīṃ Klīṃ [hsraṃ] Hsvīṃ Hsauḥ Tripuramālini Sarvamantrāsanāya Namaḥ*—thus [at the hips]. *Hrīṃ...*

"Klāṃ Kloṃ, O Siddheśvarī, beginning with Tripurā, salutation to the seat of accomplishment for the sake of the accomplishment of the goal"—thus one should place [this] at the *mūlādhāra*. Thus one should assign the six seats (*ṣaḍāsana*). "Aiṃ Klīṃ Hso, O Tripurasundarī, may you protect the self"—thus [one should recite] at the heart. "Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Hraḥ, Phaṭ to the weapon"—with this, having performed the three claps (*tāla*) and the binding of the directions, one should establish a wall of fire for the purpose of purifying the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), as has been stated.

In the case of Śrī Keśavācārya: then, having purified it with the mantra, and having performed the binding of the directions with three *tolas* of flour (*pāṇātritpaladigbandhana*) for the sake of removing obstacles, one who is wise should purify this *liṅga* consisting of the elements (*bhūtātmaka*) in due order. Then, he should cause the supreme [deity] to descend by means of the path of his own dream and by means of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of himself; that is, by means of the wind-seed-syllable (*vāyubīja*) together with the syllable *sa*.
One should burn the body with the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnivīja*).
Then, with *vaṃ*, the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, one should flood the body with nectar. With *laṃ*, the seed-syllable of earth, [one should stabilize] the limbs of the body.
One should cause [the ritual] to be performed. Then, having brought the *jīva* (vital principle) to its own place, one should practice mantra-meditation (*mantradhyāna*). It is as follows:

at the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and the center of the eyebrows, there are the circles of Fire, Sun, and Moon, consisting of ten, twelve, and sixteen petals respectively, presided over by the seed-syllables of Mūla, Vāyu, Śuṣka, Kāmarāja, and Śakti, which are mutually...

Having visualized the channels of sound as being intensely white like flashes of lightning extending up to the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), one should sprinkle one’s own body with streams of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) emerging from the form of the *mṛtakuṇḍalinī* to be described hereafter while reciting the *turīyavidyā*. Then, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs. It is as follows:

Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Tripurasundarīm aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ | Oṃ Tripurasundari anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ | Oṃ Tripurasundari kaniṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ | Oṃ Tripurasundari karapuṭābhyāṃ namaḥ | Now, because she is the mother of all mantras, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as follows:

For the Mātṛkā-nyāsa: Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*), *hnau* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*), the gods are the powers (*śakti*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Regarding the locations, it is stated in the venerable *Prapañcasāra*: "Because he is the Guru of the Seers, [Mātṛkā] is on the head; because of the syllables of the meter, [she is] on the tongue."
That which is to be understood by the intellect and not by speech is designated as the deity of the mind within the heart.
AṂ KAṂ KHAṂ GAṂ GHAṂ ḌAṂ Ā HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ | IṂ CAṂ CHAṂ JAṂ JHAṂ ÑAṂ Ī ŚIRASE SVĀHĀ | UṂ ṬAṂ ṬHAṂ ḌAṂ ḌHAṂ ṆAṂ ŚIKHĀYAI VAṢAṬ | EṂ TAṂ THAṂ DAṂ DHAṂ NAṂ E KAVACĀYA ||

HŪM! AṂ PAṂ PHAṂ BAṂ BHAṂ MAṂ AIṂ NETRĀYA VAUṢAṬ! AṂ YAṂ RAṂ LAṂ VAṂ ŚAṂ ṢAṂ SAṂ HAṂ ĀḤ ASTRĀYA PHAṬ! Having thus performed the three *tāla* strikes and the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*), one should meditate [upon the deity] with their respective mudrās. One should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): the heart with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger.
The head is touched with the thumb and ring finger; the tuft (śikhā) with a fist whose thumb is raised;
the armor (kavaca) is the touching from the eight [fingers] down to the feet with the hands in reverse position;
the eyes with the index, middle, and ring fingers; and the weapon (astra) with the snapping of the index fingers and thumbs.

"I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who has a face divided by the fifty letters, whose middle and chest are radiant and adorned with a garland, who possesses a slender waist and high breasts, who holds in her lotus-hands the seal (mudrā), a rosary for the purification of the senses, and the jar of knowledge, and who is of pure luster and three-eyed. Thus.

Having meditated thus, one should perform the *araṇyāsa* (the ritual placement on the forest). This has been stated in the venerable *Prapañcasāra*: "Indeed, [one should place] the forest (*kānana*) on the belly; the circle (*vṛtta*) on the eyes; the Vedas (*śruti*) on the cheeks; the eight (*aṣṭa*) on the roots of the teeth; the head (*mūrdhan*) on the face; the arms (*doḥ*) and feet (*pad*) on the joints (*sandhi*) and the tips (*agre*);

the two heels (*pārṣṇi-dvaya*) on the back (*pṛṣṭha*), navel (*nābhi*), and abdomen (*jaṭhara*); Rudra on the trident (*śūla*), the other [shoulder], the throat (*galaka*), and the armpits (*kakṣa*); and the fires (*agni*) on the heart."

One should assign the pervasive consciousness (*saṃjñā*) to the pair of hands and feet, and then the syllables in their proper order to the belly and the face. Then, one should cause [the consciousness] residing on the body-pīṭha to flow forth. As it was stated by the venerable Lakṣaṇadeśikendra: "The wise teacher should sequentially fashion his own body with the attributes of the pīṭhas; the learned preceptor [should place] Dharma and Jñāna upon the two shoulders and the two thighs, proceeding in a clockwise direction. Dharma, Jñāna...
Having sequentially deposited detachment and sovereignty [in the two shoulders],
one should fashion Sudharma and the others on the side of the mouth and the side of the channel; Dharma and the others are remembered as the feet.

"And others [should worship] the limbs of the seat. One should mentally project [the following] above [the heart]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to the lotus; obeisance to the solar disc; obeisance to the lunar disc; *maṃ*, obeisance to the fire-disc; *saṃ*, obeisance to Śakti; *raiṃ*, obeisance to Rāmasa; *taṃ*, obeisance to Tamas. Thus one should arrange them one above the other.
In this manner, one should contemplate the Supreme Deity within the body as consisting of the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Then, the Goddess, resembling a lotus, is as brilliant as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling the hibiscus flower, comparable to the pomegranate blossom,
resembling a ruby, and like water infused with saffron.
Adorned with a network of small bells and shimmering rubies upon her crown,
she possesses sprout-like, curling locks of hair resembling a swarm of black bees.
Her lotus-like facial orb has the appearance of the rising sun,
and upon her forehead is a soft fillet slightly curved like a half-moon.
The Supreme Goddess has the curve of her eyebrows shaped like the Pināka bow;
her eyes, filled with the joy of bliss, are swinging to and fro in playful motion.
She whose earrings are the shimmering vault of heaven, vibrating with a multitude of rays,
and whose expansive, beautiful cheeks surpass the orb of the nectar-filled moon.
The thread, fashioned by Viśvakarman and others, has a very clear heroine;
it possesses the luster of copper, coral, and the universe, and is red like a turban resembling nectar.
Her face was filled with a smile that surpassed the sweetness of the ocean of aesthetic flavors;
it was endowed with peerless qualities and graced by a beautiful chin.
The Great Goddess, with her conch-like neck, whose lovely arms are like those of Mṛḍa,
and whose lotus-hands are as delicate as the petals of a red lotus.
The ashes spread by the radiance of the nails of his lotus-like hands.
